desc:
There are n people labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry friendships[i] = [a, b] makes a and b friends. Two people are in the same friend circle if they are friends or can be linked by a chain of friends.

For every query [x, y] in queries, output 1 if x and y are in the same circle and 0 otherwise. A person is always in the same circle as themselves. Return the answers in query order.

n = 5, friendships = [[0,1],[1,2],[3,4]]
queries = [[0,2],[0,3],[3,4],[2,2]]

result = [1, 0, 1, 1]
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b, x, y < n and a ≠ b in every friendship
No pair of people appears twice in friendships
hints: All queries are about the same fixed set of friendships, so you can process the friendships once and then answer every query cheaply.
Two people are in the same circle exactly when they have the same representative in a disjoint-set structure.
Union the two endpoints of every friendship first. Then for each query compare find(x) with find(y).
editorial: Build the circles once with union-find: start with every person as their own root and union the endpoints of each friendship. Afterwards find(x) == find(y) tells whether x and y share a circle. Queries with x == y naturally answer 1.

Path compression keeps each find nearly constant, so the total time is O((n + m + q) · α(n)). Running a fresh BFS for every query would cost O(q · (n + m)), which is the thing union-find saves you from when many queries share one graph.
